sentences.gloss_en: Welcome to this explainer; let's get straight into the topic.
Today's journey starts from a slightly mathematical bit, 3D vectors, and ends with us building together an AI Data Analyst that is production-ready and well guarded with strong safety layers.
But first, how does a computer understand meaning at all?
Let's imagine a three-dimensional space, a 3D Space.
In it there is a query point moving through the space to look for its nearest neighbors.
And this is simply our roadmap; we'll go through six steps.
The steps: Meaning in Space, then The RAG Pipeline, Failures and Eval, Retrieval Security and Building Agents, and we finish with The AI Analyst.
Let's start with our first part, Meaning in Space.
Here we see the magic of embeddings: the whole idea is that we take the meaning of the text.
And we turn it into an actual physical place inside the 3D Space we imagined.
The query point keeps moving through the space until it finds its nearest neighbors.
So meaning here is literally location and distance.
To measure this closeness precisely we use the cosine similarity formula.
So what are the tools we use for search?
We have three main types.
We use lexical BM25 when we are looking for a literal match, like codes or product names.
But when the questions need understanding from meaning and concepts, dense search is the best fit.
In production, hybrid is usually the one that wins, because it takes the best of both.
And my choice of vector DB index, either Flat for accuracy or HNSW for speed.
That depends on the shape of our data, not on a trend we just follow.
Let's move on to the second section, The RAG Pipeline.
We want to picture this system like a metro line, station by station exactly.
We start by cutting documents into chunks, then we embed and index, and at the third station the query retrieves the data.
After that we must pass the Access Control Filter, then rerank the candidates, and finally the context goes to the model so it can answer.
The danger here is that any of these stations can fail and bring the whole system down.
And here is the question, predict: let's think about it together, if we asked the system in English:
Do you think the result that gets the top rank will be the right answer from the first try? What do you think?
Look at this shocking number, 0.165: this was the score of the chunk that came out first.
And the surprise is that it was talking about a roadmap that has no relation to the question at all.
The model was very confident, but wrong.
This problem we call vocabulary mismatch.
And here the retrieval process completely failed to understand what we want.
But see how the ranking shifts when we did query expansion, meaning we widened the question with a few synonyms.
Suddenly the right chunk, the one talking about idempotency, jumped to first place and its score became 0.227.
And this confirms to us that most RAG problems come from failure in the retrieval stage, not generation.
We go to the third section, Failures and Eval: for our evaluation to be right it must happen on two tracks.
First thing, did retrieval fetch the right documents at all?
And this we measure with recall@k and nDCG.
Second thing, did the generation stick to these sources, or did the model start making things up; that is groundedness.
Among the most common failures, for example, is bad chunking splitting the idea in half, so you get an incomplete answer.
Or a stale index fetching you very old data.
The fourth section is very important: Retrieval Security.
The golden rule here: retrieval is just a query, not a pass.
Meaning the forbidden chunk may be very suitable for the question in terms of meaning.
But it must be blocked at retrieval, before it reaches the model.
If we wait and the data enters the context window, then the loss is on it: the data leaked and the model saw it, done.
This is a comparison that solves a big puzzle in the field: when RAG and when fine-tuning.
We use RAG when we want to feed the system new information, like company files.
But fine-tuning we need in order to change the tone of voice, adjust the behavior, or have the model understand the terminology of a specific domain.
The two are never substitutes for each other.
The fifth section: Building Agents.
The agent, folks, is not a longer chatbot.
The chatbot at most replies to the text without remembering the state.
Whereas the agent plans, chooses the tools, keeps the state memory, and takes steps and executes them on its own.
In short, the agent needs a brain, tools, memory and a system it can plan with.
The agent lifecycle, or the agent loop, starts with evaluating the goal and choosing the tool.
But focus on this step: we must pass through the policy gate.
This gate halts execution and runs a security check to prevent any disaster before it happens.
And after that it executes, watches the result, and goes back to repeat the loop again.
And finally the sixth section, The AI Analyst.
Now let's build our ShopFlow AI Analyst.
We give it some tools like get_schema, calculate_metrics with fixed formulas, and execute_sql with a limit of 50 rows.
For safety, and the most important thing, we set the temperature to zero to make sure the generation is very accurate and logical.
And of course validation runs before any execution.
Now imagine the agent hangs and decides on its own to write a DELETE command; what will happen?
This generated command will hit hard against the first wall, which is the SQL allowlist.
Which blocks anything other than SELECT.
And if by chance it passes, it will hit the second wall, which is a read-only role on the database.
So the DELETE will be blocked and bounce back completely; that is what we call the double gate.
If we put this architecture together, we find LangChain tools secured with Pydantic.
We have a check that raises an alarm if the z-score passes 2.
And a memory that remembers only the last 10 steps.
And the most important thing, the fail-safe: max_iterations equals 10.
And this prevents the agent from entering an infinite loop or staying going around itself.
This is exactly what we achieved in this explainer: an evaluated, solid RAG with a permissions filter at retrieval.
And an analysis agent guarded with two protection layers and a full audit log of the SQL commands.
The takeaway is that real AI engineering is not only the model; it is the systems we build and secure around it.
I'll leave you to think about this question: how will you be able to secure your next autonomous AI decision in production?
Security starts from the design.
Thank you so much for completing the explainer to the end.
And let's see you in other great explainers.
